new_statements.translation: Parallel French column, same page: "C. L'accent. Nous ne marquons pas l'accent dans les textes. Nous ne savons pas encore si l'accent en ngambay est grammatical ou lexique. Certains mots semblent toujours porter un accent (sur la première voyelle): /ndāà/, /dēè/. L'accent leurs fait sembler comme si leur première voyelle avait un ton haut: /ndáà/, /déè/." (In print the second example carries a nasal hook under the e: /dēę̀/ 'they'.)

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the scanned text) and the page image also a 2x crop of the paragraph). The passage is there as quoted, in the bilingual page's English column under "C. Stress." with the parallel French "C. L'accent." column: "We do not mark stress anywhere in the texts. Whether it is grammatical or lexical remains to be discovered. Certain words seem to always carry a stress (on the first vowel); /ndāà/, /dēę̀/. This makes them sound as if the mid tone is raised to high: /ndáà/, /déę̀/." Minor differences only: the print has a semicolon (not colon) after "vowel)", and the second example carries a nasal hook under the e (/dēę̀/, /déę̀/), which the reader already notes in the translation field; the s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngambay is a three-tone language (H/M/L on every vowel and nasal). The authors do not mark stress and say it is not yet known whether stress is grammatical or lexical; the only observation is that some words (e.g. /ndaa/ 'and then', /dee/ 'they', both with a mid+low vowel sequence) seem always to carry a stress on their first vowel, perceived as the mid tone being raised to high. No general word-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('seem to', 'remains to be discovered'). Same page adds that polysyllabic words are pronounced faster so that their duration equals that of monosyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, in the context of the course texts (Moundou-town Sara-Ngambay, 1969-71 fieldwork). Tone, not stress, is the marked prosody; the 2010 GIALens sketch (southern dialect, Bibalam near Moundou) describes only tone and never mentions stress. Later phonologies (Ndjerassem 1982, 2000; Vandame 1963) were not accessible and may supersede this.
new_statements.identity_note: Thayer & Thayer 1971 describe 'Sara-Ngambay.. a dialect spoken in the town of Moundou in southern Chad' (ERIC abstract), i.e. the central Moundou variety of ngam1268 (no separate Glottolog dialect code; Glottolog dialects are Bemar, Benoye, Kere, Lara, Murum). The 2010 GIALens sketch is the southern dialect (Bibalam, near Moundou). The unopened Ndjerassem works describe the Benoye dialect (beno1238).

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing statement, which is this same passage (Vol. 3, p. 24); The IULC '506 pp.' citation is the three-volume work (232 + 156 + 115 pp. = 503 + front matter); the open_url item is Volume 1 only, which contains no stress statement. Volume 2 (micro_IA41153120_0002) has no stress/accent hits. The catalog record 'world-r2-2026-09-17' has an empty rule; the reading 'tonal with a stress statement, placement undetermined, possibly first-vowel stress on some words' is what the source supports.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngambay is a register-tone language (each vowel and nasal bears H, M or L; in a bisyllabic vowel sequence within a morpheme the first is mid and the second high or low, Vol. 3 p. 24 B 'Tone'). The authors do not mark stress and do not know whether it is grammatical (predictable) or lexical; they only observe that certain words seem always to carry a stress on their first vowel, which is heard as the mid tone being raised to high. No general placement rule is given. Volume 1's transcription conventions (pp. vii-viii) mark tone and nasalization only; there is no stress symbol and no stress statement there.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None stated. Volume 3 p. 69 (tone tendencies, section ii): in a string /M H H H M/ 'the original second /H/ might become higher than the first and third /H/, if there were emphasis, stress, or something else to raise the general pitch level' - stress is treated as a pitch-raising factor, not located.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the observation that a few words (/ndāà/ 'and then', /dēę̀/ 'they') seem always to carry a first-vowel stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Thayer & Thayer 1971 (all three volumes, ERIC abstracts and Vol. 3 front matter) describe the Sara-Ngambay of the town of Moundou, southern Chad, 'the accepted standard dialect' = ngam1268. Thayer 1978 (not opened) is by the same author on the same variety.

sources.note: Section I 'Sara-Ngambay Phonology', C. Stress (p. 24, stamped G-7): stress is not marked in the texts; whether it is grammatical or lexical 'remains to be discovered'; certain words seem always to carry a stress on the first vowel (/ndaa/ 'and then', /dee/ 'they'), which makes the mid tone sound raised to high. Tone: three levels H/M/L; each vowel and nasal carries its own tone; nasals always mid; in VV sequences first vowel mid, second high or low.
